skip_reason: Not a sales call. This is a post-move service-recovery and refund negotiation with an existing customer whose move went badly the prior day. Garrison identifies himself as operations management, not sales ('I myself and not the branch manager. I'm the operations manager, my boss his name is Frank'), takes complaint notes, negotiates a goodwill partial refund (landed at $500, quoted 3-5 business days), and schedules a no-charge fix-it crew for Wednesday 8:30-9:00 AM to move misplaced boxes upstairs and remove shrink wrap and moving-blanket trash the original crew left behind. There is no quote form, no pricing pitch, no clock explanation and no new-business booking attempt — the sales scorecard does not apply.
top_strength: Garrison ran a textbook de-escalation on a customer who opened with 'Not super happy garrison, I'm not gonna lie you.' He set expectations honestly up front about what he could and could not resolve without Frank, then took ownership without hedging or blaming the crew: 'Obviously we missed the mark pretty big-time,' 'Yes, we absolutely should have and we did not,' and 'this is entirely unacceptable. Our trash should not still be on your furniture. Shouldn't just be placed down in any random room.' He asked the customer to name her own remedy — 'as far as a partial refund though what do you think is fair?' — which let her anchor low ($700, then effectively accepting $500) instead of escalating. He also went past money to actually solving her problem, proactively offering a crew before she asked and repeating the offer with no pressure attached: 'we would love to, to make that right for you... either get out there, take all of our trash rearrange all your furniture.' He validated her evidence in real time from the photos she texted mid-call ('I can see 11 box labeled office here that obviously isn't in an office in your living room'), and explicitly refused to hide behind the internal excuse she had already been given by the crew ('she said, oh, this happens all the time and they quote us wrong' → 'Yeah, exactly, absolutely not'). Net result: an angry repeat customer demanding a refund ended the call with 'No, I appreciate it' and 'Thank you so much.'
coaching_note: Not gradeable on the sales rubric, but this call surfaces four things worth acting on. (1) Refund math does not reconcile and Garrison did the arithmetic out loud with the customer instead of from the record: she says '$1,200 with the quote and then I paid $1,900' — a $700 delta — while also volunteering 'I think I accidentally left them a tip.' Garrison offered '$500 which I think that was the difference between what you were quoted versus what, where we landed.' 'I think' is doing a lot of work there. Confirm the actual contract, invoice and tip line before the refund posts, so the customer does not get a second surprise; the line he needed was 'let me pull the exact invoice and tip line while we're on the phone so we're both working off the same number.' (2) This is an estimate-accuracy defect, not just a crew defect: she was quoted for '95 to a 115 boxes,' had two fewer large items after declining washer/dryer service, and the crew still ran out of truck room and left her garage behind — she now has to rent a U-Haul. That belongs in the estimate-accuracy review as a truck-sizing and box-count case study. (3) Crew process failures to route to branch coaching: items left in the living room rather than placed in marked rooms (including boxes labeled for a first-floor office they walked past), and shrink wrap and moving blankets left on the furniture, which is a documented standard the customer knew from her prior Einstein move. (4) Two commitments made verbally on this call now need to exist in the system — the Wednesday 8:30-9:00 AM fix-it crew (he said 'penciled in,' which is not booked) and the $500 refund. Also a process gap worth fixing: she asked for a digital receipt before paying and was told 'we can't do that,' which is what pushed her to pay while still unhappy.
phone_presence_notes: Sustained empathy and ownership under real anger with no defensiveness ('honestly I'm right there with you. This sounds absolutely unacceptable on a number of levels'), and he met her self-deprecating joke about jinxing herself with reassurance rather than plowing on ('It's not normal, it's not') — held back from a 5 only because he never got or used her name until a single late, uncertain 'Susan' at sign-off.
